Some even claimed to derive the natural sciences from the Qurʾān in the same form in which those sciences are known in our own age.
Bourgeois nationalist thought produced this new form of revivalism as another expression of the ideology of the modern Arab bourgeoisie.

To “modernize” ancient or medieval ideas and philosophies in this way, as we have said, is to treat ideas from the past as though they were identical with the ideas of the present—in this case, the twentieth century itself.
That is a metaphysical view. It denies that thought has a history and changes over time. Instead, it treats thought as static and frozen.

It also takes conditions such as capitalism, socialism, existentialism, and personalism, together with their modern meanings, out of the social relations and objective conditions that produced them in our age and transfers them into a historical setting in which they could not possibly have had any reason to exist.
This idea of complete similarity between past and present also reduces modern philosophy to something crude and simplistic.
How much would Leibniz’s mathematical thought be cheapened, for example, if we said it was simply identical with the mathematical thought of Pythagoras?
And how much would Marxist dialectical materialism be reduced if we treated it as identical with the simple materialism found among the earliest Greek materialists?
It is certainly true that no philosophy has ever appeared in a vacuum or out of nothing.
Every new philosophy has drawn on the philosophical heritage that came before it and has taken part of that earlier heritage into itself.
But this is very different from saying that old and new ideas are identical.
Hegel’s lectures on the history of philosophy help make this difference clear.

Hegel also says that contemporary philosophy is the result of all the principles that came before it. But he understands the relationship between modern philosophy and earlier philosophies—or between any later philosophy and one that came before it—through the law of the negation of the negation.
Hegel illustrates this through the natural development of a tree.
The flower, he says, negates the leaf because it shows that the leaf was not the highest stage or the full reality of the tree. The fruit then negates the flower.
Yet the fruit could never exist if all the earlier stages—root, leaf, and flower—had not come before it.

The appearance of these currents and others like them in an age of national liberation movements and the collapse of imperialism, together with the growing intensity of ideological struggle, has pushed the question of our position toward the national intellectual heritage to the front of the issues facing our time.
We now have to evaluate this heritage, understand it, and put it to use within that ideological struggle itself.
For this reason, the question has become more complex at the same time as it has become one of the central problems of modern thought.
At the present stage, it can no longer be solved without an ideological basis.
Arab bourgeois thought is trying to solve the problem through the kinds of answers we have just described, in keeping with its own ideological position.

It is therefore time for revolutionary Arab thought to offer its own answers, based on its own revolutionary ideology: the ideology of the classes and social groups standing against the camp of the reactionary right-wing bourgeoisie, which opposes the development of the national liberation movement in a socially democratic and revolutionary direction.

As we have seen from some of the examples above, bourgeois solutions to the problem of heritage reveal not only the ideological confusion of the bourgeoisie. They also reveal its inability to come to terms with the spirit of modern science.
This failure may itself reflect the ideological confusion into which the profound changes of our age have thrown it.

From our point of view, a genuinely scientific and objective attempt to evaluate the national intellectual heritage and absorb it in the true spirit of our age must lead to the conclusion that this problem can be solved correctly only on the basis of the Marxist-Leninist method.
This method requires us to bring out the democratic content that lies within every national intellectual heritage and connect it with the international democratic content of modern culture.

That modern democratic content is itself a real reflection of the international democratic content of today’s national liberation revolutions and of the socialist revolution that has become one of the defining features of our age.

From these conclusions, we can see that a scientific solution to the relationship between our Arab present—with all its national, social, and intellectual dimensions—and the intellectual heritage of our past depends on our having a clear scientific understanding of two facts.
The first is the revolutionary content of the Arab national liberation movement today and the direction of its future development.
The second is the deep connection between the revolutionary character of that movement and the need for a revolutionary position toward the heritage.
In other words, our position toward the heritage must begin from the present itself—from the revolutionary side of that present.
The first point becomes clear when we look closely at the overall direction of the Arab national liberation movement, especially from the period after the Second World War down to the present.
If we drew a graph of its recent course, we would see that its upward movement has generally been stronger than its downward movement.
We would also see that the upward curve is revolutionary in its basic character.
It gains this character from the growing national and social awareness of liberation among the Arab popular masses. This awareness appears in several ways.

First, there is a deepening hostility toward colonialism and imperialism, and toward the forces that cooperate with them, depend on them, or take part with them in seizing the national rights of peoples, taking their land and resources, and suppressing their national aspirations for liberation.
This includes international Zionism and the state it established through the seizure of Palestine.

Second, through different forms and levels of struggle, this hostility is increasingly becoming hostility toward the social system represented by colonialism and imperialism—that is, the system of capitalist exploitation.
Third, under the influence of these two factors and of social conditions in most Arab countries, this awareness has increasingly taken the form of class consciousness as well.
The national character of the struggle of the Arab masses is therefore increasingly joined by a social character, to the point that the dividing line between the two is becoming difficult to see.

In recent years, we have therefore seen the struggles of the masses in different places rise to a more advanced level, where the goals of national liberation and social liberation increasingly overlap and become inseparable. Lebanon provides one example.
Fourth, the development of national and political awareness in this way has begun to produce a noticeable change inside the Arab national liberation movement itself.
The relationship between two of its main sides is beginning to break apart.
The first consists of some senior leaders of certain Arab regimes and the supporters they draw from the “new class” created by those regimes.

The second consists of workers, poor peasants, revolutionary intellectuals, soldiers, and broad sections of the lower and middle bourgeoisie, influenced by the work of national and progressive parties and forces.
The developments we have described did not take place in isolation.

They were connected with the victories won by many national liberation movements in Southeast Asia and Africa, with the struggles of the international revolutionary movement in the capitalist countries, and with the deep social, intellectual, and political influence exercised across the world by the victorious leading force of that movement: the socialist system of states.

Taken together, these conditions have produced a clear difference in position between the two main sides of the Arab national liberation movement over the national causes to which that movement is committed, above all the complete national liberation of the Palestinian Arab people.
This difference became especially visible during the 1970s.

Signs began to appear that the first side might lay down the weapons of struggle against imperialism—especially American imperialism—and against the forces allied with or dependent on it, including Zionism and Arab reaction.
It had begun, or was close to beginning, to abandon its position in the Arab liberation struggle and move toward the position of its real enemies.

Yet opposition to imperialism and its allies and dependents had originally formed the basis of the temporary alliance between the different forces within the Arab national liberation movement as a whole.
The popular, national, and progressive forces that make up the other side have moved in the opposite direction.
As the struggle develops, they become more firmly rooted in their position and more deeply committed to its revolutionary demands.

At the same time, the leaders of the first side and the forces supporting them increasingly redirect their main conflict away from the enemies of national liberation and toward the friends of those same national causes.
This growing difference in position has revealed the social and class foundations behind it.
It has also brought more clearly to the surface the meaning of the close and inseparable connection between national struggle and social struggle within the Arab national liberation movement.
In doing so, it has confirmed the revolutionary content that is becoming ever more deeply rooted within that movement.
Fifth, there are the continuing changes taking place within fighting groups that form part of the Arab national liberation movement.
Some of these groups originally emerged at an earlier stage with chauvinistic, racial, and isolationist nationalist ideas, along with ways of thinking closer to a new form of revivalism.
Their response to the later changes, both in theory and in practice, means two things.
First, they are freeing themselves from their earlier ideas and tendencies.
Second, through revolutionary conviction, they are choosing to merge themselves into the scientific course of the revolutionary movement and into the practical struggle that follows that course.

Sixth, the main forces of the Arab national liberation movement increasingly understand that there is an unavoidable and fundamental connection of principle and destiny between themselves and the other national liberation movements of the world, as well as with the international revolutionary movement as a whole and its firm leading force: the system of socialist countries.
These are the main elements that make up the content of the Arab national liberation movement at its present stage.
As we can see, this content contains a number of revolutionary elements.
This does not mean that we ignore, overlook, or underestimate the negative elements that also exist within the movement.
It means only that we are identifying its general direction and the future possibilities contained within it: a conscious revolutionary development rather than a merely spontaneous one.

We now come to the second point: the deep connection between the revolutionary content of the Arab national liberation movement at its present stage and a revolutionary position toward the Arab-Islamic intellectual heritage.
What do we mean by this?
And why do we call it a fact?
Something does not become true simply because we want it to be true.
Truth is not subjective. It is objective. Otherwise it is not truth at all, but an illusion, an idea, an opinion, or a vision.
This is the heart of the issue before us.
The connection we are talking about is a real and objective one. It is therefore genuinely a fact.
It would be unnatural—if not impossible—for us to take a revolutionary position toward the problems of the present while taking a non-revolutionary position toward the heritage of the past.
A revolutionary outlook cannot be divided up in that way.
To divide it here is to destroy the whole position and reveal that the claimed “revolutionary” outlook is only something artificially attached to the field to which it claims to belong.
A revolutionary position toward the problems of the present requires us to begin from that same position when looking at the heritage.
That means knowing the heritage in a revolutionary way and building that knowledge on the ideology of the revolutionary forces of the present.
These are the forces that have an objective historical relationship with the social basis on which the intellectual heritage of the past was produced.
By this we mean the earlier social forces that produced the material foundations reflected in the forms of social consciousness—philosophy, science, literature, and art—that make up this heritage.
Building our knowledge of the heritage on this ideological basis is not something we are forcing onto reality from outside, nor is it something produced by pure abstract reasoning.
It comes from the nature of reality itself.

If we examine—as we will later in this introduction—the different ways in which people have understood our intellectual heritage through history, interpretation, or study in the various periods that came after it, we will find many different forms of knowledge.
Some differ from one another. Some directly contradict one another. Others resemble one another.

Why does one historian understand the heritage differently from another? Why does one interpreter or researcher reach a different understanding from another, when the inherited intellectual work itself remains the same historical reality?
Its texts have been handed down in fixed form to later generations, whether those texts have already been discovered or are still unknown to us.
To explain this, we must first distinguish between the heritage itself and our knowledge of the heritage.
